input:
This example calculates the net radiative heat flux leaving a furnace wall facing much cooler surroundings. The quantity we are interested in is the net radiative heat flux, denoted by $q$ and expressed in kW m-2, and it depends on the emissivity of the wall surface, denoted by $\varepsilon$, on the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, denoted by $\sigma$, which has the value 5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4, and on the temperatures of the wall and of the surroundings, denoted by $T_1$ and $T_2$ respectively. In the present case, the wall is at a temperature of 1000 K and the surroundings are at 350 K. The relationship connecting all of these quantities to one another is the following equation:

$$q = \varepsilon \sigma (T_1^4 - T_2^4)$$

The emissivity of the wall surface is 0.85, a value which reflects the fact that the surface does not radiate quite as effectively as a perfect emitter would at the same temperature. Substituting all of the values into the equation and carrying out the calculation gives a net radiative heat flux of 47.5 kW m-2. The result is dominated by the wall temperature because each temperature enters the equation raised to the fourth power, so the contribution from the hot wall is much larger than that coming back from the cooler surroundings, and the net flux is the difference between a large emitted term and a small received term. It should be borne in mind, however, that this estimate rests on a simplifying treatment in which both surfaces are regarded as large and parallel, so that every part of each surface faces the other. View factors for the real geometry are not included in the calculation, and in an actual furnace, where parts of the wall may face surfaces that are shielded or colder, the exchange that takes place could well be less than the value that has been obtained here.
target:
The net radiative heat flux $q$ (kW m-2) from a furnace wall is calculated from the wall emissivity $\varepsilon$ (dimensionless), the Stefan-Boltzmann constant $\sigma$ (5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4), the wall temperature $T_1$ (1000 K) and the surroundings temperature $T_2$ (350 K) by

$$q = \varepsilon \sigma (T_1^4 - T_2^4)$$

Net flux is emission less return: the wall radiates toward the surroundings and receives radiation back, and $q$ is the difference. The wall emissivity is 0.85, the share of perfect-emitter radiation the surface achieves at its temperature. Substitution gives $q$ = 47.5 kW m-2. Each temperature enters at the fourth power, so the hotter temperature dominates the exchange and the return from the surroundings offsets only a small part of what the wall emits; at equal temperatures the two terms would cancel and the net flux would vanish, which is the check the stated value has to pass in direction. The constant carries the units it does because the flux it scales is an energy flow per unit area, and the fourth-power law leaves it no simpler form.

The estimate treats both surfaces as large and parallel, so every part of each surface faces the other. View factors for the real geometry are not included, and a wall part facing shielded or colder surfaces would exchange less than the stated flux. The value is the large-parallel-surface result at the stated temperatures and emissivity. Emissivity is the one property of the surface in the calculation, and it enters as a simple multiplier: a surface that emits less freely gives a proportionally smaller flux at the same temperatures.
